column2: Text split into tokens (word/sub-word units) — tokens ≠ words.
Each token mapped to a numeric vector capturing meaning.
Added to embeddings so word order is preserved.
Each token weighs the relevance of every other token, regardless of distance — the defining transformer innovation, giving both long-range context and efficient parallel training.
Per-token transformation applied after attention.

column1: Embedding vs. vector vs. vector database?
column2: Embedding = semantic representation; vector = the numeric array it's stored as; vector database = where those arrays are stored/searched (e.g., Amazon OpenSearch Service, Aurora + pgvector, Amazon Kendra).

column1: Embedding model choice — general-purpose sufficient, or poor retrieval quality?
column2: Sufficient → general-purpose model (e.g., Titan Text Embeddings), $, lowest latency. Poor retrieval but not domain-specialized → larger general model or better chunking/hybrid search, $$.

column1: Embedding model choice — domain-specialized: fine-tune or not?
column2: Fine-tuning not justified → domain-specific pretrained embedding model, $$. Justified (large labeled dataset, high-stakes accuracy) → fine-tune an embedding model (e.g., via SageMaker), $$$ — jumping straight here "to be safe" usually just adds cost.

Cost: per-token (on-demand) or Provisioned Throughput, bigger/more capable models cost more per token. Modality: does the model accept/produce the needed input/output types (text, image, audio, video)?

column1: FM selection factors — latency & context window?
column2: Latency: real-time/interactive use cases need fast (usually smaller) models, batch/async tolerates more. Context window: is the input (plus retrieved context) small enough to fit without chunking?

column1: FM selection factors — fine-tuning support & model size/accuracy/licensing?
column2: Can the model/provider be fine-tuned or continued-pre-trained if needed? Parameter count is a rough capability/cost proxy; validate accuracy with Amazon Bedrock Model Evaluation; check compliance/licensing terms.
Text → text; lowest cost/latency; high-volume, cheap, latency-sensitive text (simple chat, classification).
Text/image/video → text; low cost; lightweight multimodal chat, document Q&A with images.
Text/image/video → text; moderate cost; balanced multimodal RAG, moderate agentic reasoning.
Text/image/video → text; highest cost; most complex multi-step multimodal reasoning; teacher model for distillation.
Text/image → image; priced per image; studio-quality image generation/editing.
Text/image → video; priced per second; short-form video generation (async).
Speech → speech; priced per duration; real-time speech-to-speech (voice assistants, IVR).
Ask the model to perform a task with no examples; does not change model weights.

Instruct the model to reason step by step before the final answer; does not change model weights.
Tell the model what not to include or do (common in image generation); does not change model weights.
Retrains the model's weights on labeled examples — the only one of these that changes weights.
A reusable prompt structure with placeholders for variable content.
Malicious input tries to override a prompt's original instructions; mitigated with input validation + Guardrails for Amazon Bedrock.

column1: What are the four parts of a well-formed prompt?

Randomness of next-token choice; low = focused/deterministic, high = creative/varied.

column1: Top-p (nucleus sampling) — what does it control?
column2: Cumulative-probability candidate pool; low = narrower/safer, high = wider/more diverse.
Fixed-size candidate pool of k most-likely tokens; small k = safer/less varied, large k = more diverse.

column1: Max tokens — what does it control?
column2: Cap on response length; low = shorter (may truncate), high = longer responses allowed.

column1: Stop sequences — what do they control?
column2: Halt generation when a matched string appears — immediate stop, no gradient.

column1: Order of operations & exam trap — temperature/top-p/top-k?
column2: Temperature reshapes the distribution first, then top-p/top-k prune the candidate pool, then the next token is sampled — not independent dials. So low temp + high top-p/top-k is still mostly deterministic, and high temp + low top-p/top-k is still narrow/repetitive.

column1: Do inference parameters reduce hallucination or enforce a content policy?
column2: No — only RAG (facts) and Guardrails for Amazon Bedrock (safety) do that.
Max tokens and stop sequences are the direct levers; lower temperature indirectly cuts JSON/format retries and completion length without changing per-token price.
Source documents (e.g., product catalog, policy docs) loaded from a data source — Amazon S3, SharePoint, Salesforce.
Documents split into chunks; each chunk converted to an embedding vector via an embeddings model (e.g., Amazon Titan Text Embeddings).
Vectors stored in a vector store for similarity search — Amazon OpenSearch Service, Aurora + pgvector, Amazon Kendra.
The user's question is embedded the same way, using the same embeddings model.
Vector store returns the chunks closest (most similar) to the query vector; managed by Knowledge Bases for Amazon Bedrock.
Retrieved chunks + original question passed as a prompt to an LLM (e.g., Claude, Titan), which generates a grounded answer.
No — RAG grounds answers in retrieved data at inference time; this is what distinguishes it from fine-tuning.
Reduce hallucination by grounding output in actual source data — it does not fully restore interpretability or guarantee correctness.

column1: Fabricated/wrong facts vs. wrong tone/format/style — which needs RAG?
column2: Fabricated facts → RAG. Wrong tone/format/style → prompt engineering or fine-tuning, not RAG.
The managed, no-retrain way to wire the RAG pipeline (ingest → retrieve → generate) together without building custom retrieval code.
One FM handles many tasks (summarization, drafting, Q&A, code) via prompting alone.
Interactive, real-time conversational responses (chatbots, assistants).
Produces novel content/ideas instead of just a label or number.
One deployed FM serves many use cases/users, versus dozens of bespoke models.
Fluent, confident output that is factually incorrect or fabricated (e.g., a citation/API that doesn't exist); primary mitigation is RAG (lower temperature helps marginally).
Black box — hard to explain why an FM produced a given output; mitigated by human review, not inference parameters.
Output is simply wrong/outdated/low quality, distinct from confident fabrication; mitigated by model evaluation, RAG, fine-tuning on better data.
Same prompt → different outputs on different runs; mitigated by lowering temperature/top-p/top-k (reduces, doesn't eliminate).
Large FMs, long context windows, and retries can be expensive at scale; mitigated by right-sizing the model, capping max tokens, lowering temperature to cut retries.

Malicious input overrides/manipulates the original prompt instructions; mitigated by input validation + Guardrails for Amazon Bedrock (configurable safety/compliance filters — harmful content, denied topics, PII redaction — applied consistently across models).
Hallucination is confidently fabricating specifics; inaccuracy is just being wrong/low quality — the exam tests this distinction directly.

"Up-to-date/proprietary data without retraining" → RAG; "specific tone, format, or labeled task" → fine-tuning; full pretraining of a new FM is almost never the correct answer for a business use case.

column1: Confused pair: lowering temperature vs. eliminating hallucination?
column2: Lowering temperature reduces nondeterminism but does not eliminate hallucination risk — that comes from training data/RAG, not sampling.
Top-p = cumulative-probability threshold; top-k = fixed count of top tokens — don't swap these under pressure.

column1: Confused pair: few-shot prompting vs. fine-tuning?
column2: Few-shot prompting changes nothing about model weights; only fine-tuning retrains them.

column1: Exam trap: scenario states multiple constraints at once (e.g., real-time + long documents + fixed budget)?
column2: Weigh all of them together — don't just pick the biggest/most capable model.

column1: Confused pair: PartyRock vs. Amazon Q Business vs. SageMaker JumpStart?
column2: No-code, quick experimentation = PartyRock; pre-built, grounded in enterprise data out of the box = Amazon Q Business; deep infra control/mix with SageMaker = SageMaker JumpStart.

column1: Numeric/scope trap: "one company, five initiatives" business scenario?
column2: Map each stated initiative to exactly one use case and one AWS service, never more than one of each.

column1: Confused pair: RAG vs. fine-tuning vs. continued pre-training — which touch model weights?
column2: RAG never touches weights (grounds at inference time); fine-tuning retrains weights on labeled task data; continued pre-training retrains weights on unlabeled domain corpora.
